claim: Recent developments in human neuroimaging make it possible to non-invasively measure neural activity from different cortical layers.
source: Recent developments in human neuroimaging make it possible to non-invasively measure neural activity from different cortical layers.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on laminar fMRI methods.

claim: Bottom-up and top-down responses are associated with distinct laminar profiles.
source: Specifically, bottom-up and top-down responses are associated with distinct laminar profiles.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge and cited literature.

claim: BOLD responses were modulated by both stimulus contrast (bottom-up) and by engaging feature-based attention (top-down).
source: BOLD responses were modulated by both stimulus contrast (bottom-up) and by engaging feature-based attention (top-down).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Bottom-up modulations were strongest in the middle cortical layer and weaker in deep and superficial layers.
source: Bottom-up modulations were strongest in the middle cortical layer and weaker in deep and superficial layers
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Top-down modulations were strongest in the superficial layers.
source: top-down modulations were strongest in the superficial layers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Laminar activity profiles can discriminate between concurrent top-down and bottom-up processing.
source: As such, we demonstrate that laminar activity profiles can discriminate between concurrent top-down and bottom-up processing, and are diagnostic of how a brain region is activated.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claim: Using 'ultra-high field' MRI systems of 7T and above, it has become possible to non-invasively measure fMRI responses at lamina-resolved spatial resolutions in humans.
source: Using 'ultra-high field' MRI systems of 7T and above, it has become possible to non-invasively measure fMRI responses at lamina-resolved spatial resolutions in humans (Dumoulin et al., 2018; Koopmans et al., 2011; Polimeni et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Bottom-up connections between brain areas target the granular layer 4, at middle cortical depths.
source: Bottom-up connections between brain areas are known to target the granular layer 4, at middle cortical depths, while top-down connections target deeper and superficial layers but largely avoid layer 4 (Anderson and Martin, 2009; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical literature.

claim: Top-down connections target deeper and superficial layers but largely avoid layer 4.
source: Bottom-up connections between brain areas are known to target the granular layer 4, at middle cortical depths, while top-down connections target deeper and superficial layers but largely avoid layer 4 (Anderson and Martin, 2009; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical literature.

claim: Stimulus-driven responses in visual cortex have been shown to be strongest at middle depths.
source: For example, stimulus-driven responses in visual cortex have been shown to be strongest at middle depths (Koopmans et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Top-down signals embodying contextual inference, prediction, attention and working memory operate at deep and/or superficial, but not middle, cortical depths.
source: while top-down signals embodying contextual inference, prediction, attention and working memory operate at deep and/or superficial, but not middle, cortical depths (Klein et al., 2018; Kok et al., 2016; Lawrence et al., 2018; Muckli et al., 2015; Scheeringa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Similar results for top-down influences have been reported for auditory cortex.
source: Similar results for top-down influences have also been reported for auditory (De Martino et al., 2015) and motor cortex (Huber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Similar results for top-down influences have been reported for motor cortex.
source: Similar results for top-down influences have also been reported for auditory (De Martino et al., 2015) and motor cortex (Huber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Subjects performed at 83.5% correct (SD = 2.3) for low contrast stimuli.
source: On average, subjects performed at 83.5% correct (SD = 2.3) for low and 84.5% correct (SD = 1.5) for high contrast stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from the experiment.

claim: Subjects performed at 84.5% correct (SD = 1.5) for high contrast stimuli.
source: On average, subjects performed at 83.5% correct (SD = 2.3) for low and 84.5% correct (SD = 1.5) for high contrast stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from the experiment.

claim: The difference in task performance between high and low contrast stimuli was significant (t [22]=2.52, p=0.019).
source: Despite this, the numerically small difference in task performance was significant (t [22]=2.52, p=0.019).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Responses to high contrast stimuli were significantly higher than low contrast stimuli across V1-V3 (F [23, 1]=35.57, p=4.00e−6).
source: Responses to high contrast stimuli were significantly higher than low contrast stimuli across V1-V3 (F [23, 1]=35.57, p=4.00e−6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The size of the contrast effect varied across areas (F [30.2, 1.3]=46.53, p=1.77e−8), being larger in V1 than V2 and V3.
source: The size of this effect varied across areas (F [30.2, 1.3]=46.53, p=1.77e−8), being larger in V1 than V2 and V3.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Voxel responses were higher when their preferred orientation was attended, compared to when the orthogonal orientation was attended (F [23, 1]=25.67, p=4.00e−5).
source: Voxel responses were also higher when their preferred orientation was attended, compared to when the orthogonal orientation was attended (F [23, 1]=25.67, p=4.00e−5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The attention effect varied across visual areas (F [46, 2]=4.91, p=0.012), being slightly smaller in V1 compared to V2 and V3.
source: This effect also varied across visual areas (F [46, 2]=4.91, p=0.012), being slightly smaller in V1 compared to V2 and V3.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The effect of feature-based attention on neural responses was present at all cortical depths and was largest in the superficial layers.
source: Within this time window, the effect of feature-based attention on neural responses was present at all cortical depths and was largest in the superficial layers (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There was a trend of activity differences between layers induced by the attentional manipulation (F [46, 2]=2.82, p=0.070).
source: There was a trend of activity differences between layers induced by the attentional manipulation (F [46, 2]=2.82, p=0.070).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The attentional modulation was significantly stronger in the superficial layers compared to the middle (t [23]=2.11, p=0.046) and deep layers (t [23]=2.15, p=0.042).
source: Unpacking this, the attentional modulation was significantly stronger in the superficial layers compared to the middle (t [23]=2.11, p=0.046) and deep layers (t [23]=2.15, p=0.042)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There was no significant difference in the strength of the attentional modulation between the deep and middle layers (t [23]=0.36, p=0.723).
source: while there was no significant difference in the strength of the attentional modulation between the deep and middle layers (t [23]=0.36, p=0.723).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Contrast modulations varied significantly across depth (F [46, 2]=8.43, p=0.001), being largest at middle compared to deep (t [23]=3.79, p=0.001) and superficial (t [23]=3.56, p=0.002) depths.
source: Indeed, contrast modulations varied significantly across depth (F [46, 2]=8.43, p=0.001), being largest at middle compared to deep (t [23]=3.79, p=0.001) and superficial (t [23]=3.56, p=0.002) depths.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The organization of contrast-related modulations across depth was significantly different to those caused by feature-based attention, as shown by a source (bottom-up, top-down) X layer (deep, middle, superficial) interaction (F [46, 2]=4.39, p=0.018).
source: Critically, the organization of contrast-related modulations across depth was significantly different to those caused by feature-based attention, as shown by a source (bottom-up, top-down) X layer (deep, middle, superficial) interaction (F [46, 2]=4.39, p=0.018).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Feature-based attention effects were more agranular compared to stimulus contrast (t [23]=3.11, p=0.005).
source: As predicted, feature-based attention effects were more agranular compared to stimulus contrast (Figure 3E). This difference was significant (t [23]=3.11, p=0.005)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 20 of 24 subjects showed an effect where attention was more agranular than contrast.
source: and 20 of our 24 subjects showed an effect in this direction (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by individual subject data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Variation in the effect of attention across depth over V1-V3 did not reach significance (F [46, 2]=2.54, p=0.090).
source: Similar to our original analysis, variation in the effect of attention across depth over V1-V3 (Figure 4A) did not reach significance (F [46, 2]=2.54, p=0.090)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Attention depth profiles were similar across areas (F [69.67, 3.03]=0.44 p=0.778).
source: and attention depth profiles were similar across areas (F [69.67, 3.03]=0.44 p=0.778).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The effect of contrast varied across cortical depth (F [36.28, 1.58]=7.52, p=0.004) peaking at middle depths.
source: The effect of contrast did vary across cortical depth (F [36.28, 1.58]=7.52, p=0.004) peaking at middle depths (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The contrast depth profile was not significantly different between the three areas (F [92, 4]=1.39, p=0.244).
source: but this profile was not significantly different between the three areas (F [92, 4]=1.39, p=0.244.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There was an overall, area independent, difference between feature-based attention and stimulus contrast that approached significance (F [46, 2]=2.74, p=0.075).
source: When directly contrasting these two modulatory factors, there was an overall, area independent, difference between feature-based attention and stimulus contrast that approached significance (F [46, 2]=2.74, p=0.075)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There were no significant differences between areas in the attention-contrast comparison (F [80.38, 3.50]=1.00, p=0.407).
source: but no significant differences between areas (F [80.38, 3.50]=1.00, p=0.407).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In general, modulations from feature-based attention were more agranular compared to those from stimulus contrast (F [23, 1]=5.48, p=0.028).
source: In general, modulations from feature-based attention were more agranular compared to those from stimulus contrast (F [23, 1]=5.48, p=0.028)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The agranular-granular difference was consistent across visual areas (F [46, 2]=0.51, p=0.607).
source: and this was consistent across visual areas (F [46, 2]=0.51, p=0.607).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Twenty-six healthy participants completed the experiment.
source: Twenty-six healthy participants (all right-handed, nine males, mean age 25.5, age range 19–47) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision completed the experiment.
evidence: Reported participant demographics.

claim: The sample size (N = 26) provided 80% power to detect one-sided experimental effects that had at least medium effect size (Cohen's d > 0.6).
source: This sample size (N = 26) provided us with 80% power to detect one-sided experimental effects that had at least medium effect size (Cohen's d > 0.6).
evidence: Based on power calculation.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committees (CMO region Arnhem-Nijmegen, The Netherlands, and ethics committee of the University Duisburg-Essen, Germany, protocol CMO 2014/288).
source: All gave written informed consent and the study was approved by the local ethics committees (CMO region Arnhem-Nijmegen, The Netherlands, and ethics committee of the University Duisburg-Essen, Germany, protocol CMO 2014/288).
evidence: Reported ethical approval.

claim: The experiment and analysis plan were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/46adc/).
source: The experiment and analysis plan were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/46adc/).
evidence: Reported preregistration.

claim: Influences of feature-based attention have been reported in the LGN before.
source: Interestingly, influences of feature-based attention have been reported in the LGN before (Ling et al., 2015; Schneider, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: van Kerkoerle et al. (2017) report increased spike rate and current sinks with attention that were largest in the agranular layers.
source: van Kerkoerle et al. (2017) report increased spike rate and current sinks with attention that were largest in the agranular layers.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Van Kerkoerle et al. report strong attentional modulations in the deep layers compared to the middle layer.
source: In particular, Van Kerkoerle et al. report strong attentional modulations in the deep layers compared to the middle layer, which was not the case in our data.
evidence: Comparison to cited study and current data.

claim: Other studies report attentional effects on spike rate in all layers of V1.
source: Other studies (Denfield et al., 2018; Hembrook-Short et al., 2017) report attentional effects on spike rate in all layers of V1.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nandy et al. (2017) report attentional modulations in all layers of V4.
source: Nandy et al. (2017) report attentional modulations in all layers of V4, consistent with our findings in extrastriate areas V2 and V3, as well as V1
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Buffalo et al. (2011) report attentional modulation of gamma and alpha oscillations in deep and superficial cortex that were similar in V1, V2 and V4.
source: Buffalo et al. (2011) report attentional modulation of gamma and alpha oscillations in deep and superficial cortex that were similar in V1, V2 and V4.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Gradient-echo BOLD suffers from a bias in signal strength whereby responses in superficial cortex are stronger than responses from deep cortex.
source: It is well established that gradient-echo BOLD suffers from a bias in signal strength whereby responses in superficial cortex are stronger than responses from deep cortex (Koopmans et al., 2010; Uğurbil et al., 2003; Uludağ and Blinder, 2018; Yacoub et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Plaid stimuli comprised two orthogonal sets of bars (one oriented 45°, one oriented 135°).
source: We report laminar-resolved fMRI responses from the early visual cortex (V1-V3) of 24 healthy human subjects while they viewed a series of plaid stimuli comprising two orthogonal sets of bars (one oriented 45°, hereafter referred to as 'clockwise', the other oriented 135°, hereafter referred to as 'counter-clockwise'; see Figure 1).
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli shown in Figure 1.

claim: Participants monitored changes in bar width of either the clockwise or counter-clockwise bars.
source: Plaids were presented in blocks of 8 stimuli, during which participants monitored changes in bar width of either the clockwise or counter-clockwise bars (Kamitani and Tong, 2005).
evidence: Description of experimental task.

claim: Both sets of bars varied in width independently of each other, meaning attention had to be focused on the cued orientation to succeed at the task.
source: Importantly, both sets of bars varied in width independently of each other, meaning attention had to be focused on the cued orientation to succeed at the task.
evidence: Description of task design.

claim: Each block of stimuli comprised either high (80%) or low (30%) contrast plaid stimuli.
source: Stimulus contrast was also manipulated: each block of stimuli comprised either high (80%) or low (30%) contrast plaid stimuli.
evidence: Description of experimental manipulation.

claim: Laminar fMRI is well suited to exploring laminar differences between brain areas as it affords simultaneous measurements over larger areas of cortex compared to electrophysiological methods.
source: For future studies, laminar fMRI is well suited to exploring laminar differences between brain areas as it affords simultaneous measurements over larger areas of cortex compared to electrophysiological methods.
evidence: Inference about methodological advantages.

claim: Top-down effects can be separated from concurrent bottom-up modulations driven by the stimulus by orthogonally manipulating stimulus contrast and feature-based attention.
source: By orthogonally manipulating stimulus contrast and feature-based attention, we have shown that top-down effects can be separated from concurrent bottom-up modulations driven by the stimulus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claim: Each stimulus is expected to trigger a large response in the middle layer of V1 driven by bottom-up connections from the LGN.
source: Each stimulus is expected to trigger a large response in the middle layer of V1 driven by bottom-up connections from the LGN (Hubel and Wiesel, 1972).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge and cited literature.

claim: The relatively similar strength of attentional modulations across cortical layers could be due to blurring of BOLD responses across depth bins from spatial hemodynamics.
source: It is possible that we found top-down effects were similar across cortical depth due the blurring of BOLD responses across depth bins from spatial hemodynamics.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed results.

claim: Repeated visual stimulation could have effectively washed out depth-specific responses, increasing the likelihood of experimental effects being uniform across depth.
source: It is therefore possible that repeated visual stimulation could have effectively washed out depth-specific responses, increasing the likelihood of experimental effects being uniform across depth.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed results.

claim: Any influence of spatial hemodynamics should be consistent across experimental conditions, and therefore accounted for in the calculation of bottom-up/top-down modulations via a subtraction of the responses to different contrast/attention conditions.
source: That said, any influence of spatial hemodynamics should be consistent across experimental conditions, and therefore accounted for in our calculation of bottom-up/top-down modulations via a subtraction of the responses to different contrast/attention conditions.
evidence: Inference about methodological control.

claim: The strikingly distinct laminar profile of stimulus contrast effects that clearly peaked in the middle layers indicates that the analysis could account for the influence of hemodynamics.
source: Indeed, the strikingly distinct laminar profile of stimulus contrast effects that clearly peaked in the middle layers indicates that our analysis could account for the influence of hemodynamics.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data.

claim: Accurate depth-estimates of BOLD responses continues to be the biggest challenge in laminar fMRI.
source: Nevertheless, accurate depth-estimates of BOLD responses continues to be the biggest challenge in laminar fMRI.
evidence: Statement about methodological challenges based on field knowledge.

claim: For stimulus contrast, the similarity across areas is consistent with a purely stimulus-driven effect that changes response amplitude at early, subcortical levels and is inherited through the visual system via bottom-up connections targeting layer 4.
source: For stimulus contrast, this is consistent with a purely stimulus-driven effect that changes response amplitude at early, subcortical levels and is inherited through the visual system via bottom-up connections targeting layer 4 (Hubel and Wiesel, 1972; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: Inference based on data and cited anatomical knowledge.
